passage:
12 March, night
Prashant found the loan papers today. He didn't shout, which was worse. He just asked, "Why?" and I heard myself say, "Because you would never have agreed." His face closed like a door. I meant it as the truth, but it came out as if I was blaming him for my lie.
The truth is messier. When Sharmila bhabhi called crying that the landlord would shut Bhaiya's shop, I thought of Papa telling us as kids that a sister never counts favours for her brother. And then I thought of Prashant's face last year when my cousin borrowed money, and the long lecture after. So I signed, and every month I paid it from my salary and said nothing.
I'm ashamed. I'm also angry that I felt I had to hide it. Both are true tonight.
Mahima

qa.q: What did Mahima say when Prashant asked 'Why?'
qa.a: Mahima said, 'Because you would never have agreed.'

qa.q: What mixed feelings is Mahima writing about at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Mahima feels ashamed of hiding the loan and also angry that she felt she had to hide it; she writes that both are true tonight.

qa.q: What could Mahima do next so her defence stops adding to Prashant's hurt?
qa.a: Mahima could go back and say plainly that hiding it was wrong, without 'you would never have agreed', and then explain her fear and her brother's trouble as context, not as an excuse.

qa.q: How might Prashant have heard Mahima's answer?
qa.a: Prashant likely heard it as blame, as if his temper caused her secret, which made the hurt worse; that is why his face 'closed like a door'.

grounding: Shows the wife torn between family loyalty and fear of her husband's reaction, and how her defence that he would never have agreed deepens his hurt.

passage:
Vaibhav: Your brother just thanked me for "the help with the loan". What loan, Yamini?
Yamini: I was going to tell you.
Vaibhav: When? It's been a year.
Yamini: He had nowhere else to go. Mummy was calling me every night, crying.
Vaibhav: You could have come to me.
Yamini: You would never have agreed. You know that.
Vaibhav: So it's my fault that my wife signed a loan behind my back?
Yamini: I didn't say that.
Yamini: I just knew you'd look at me the way you're looking at me now. Like I'm stupid for helping my own family.
Vaibhav: I'm not looking at you. I'm sitting in the car downstairs because I can't come up yet.
Yamini: I'm sorry. I was scared.
Vaibhav: Scared of me? That's worse, Yamini.
Neither of them typed anything for a long time.

qa.q: Where is Vaibhav while he is typing?
qa.a: Vaibhav is sitting in the car downstairs.

qa.q: Why did Yamini hide the loan, going by her messages?
qa.a: Yamini felt pulled by her family, with Mummy calling every night, and was scared Vaibhav would judge her as stupid for helping them.

qa.q: What could Yamini say instead of 'you would never have agreed' to open a way forward?
qa.a: Yamini could own the choice plainly, for example 'Hiding it was wrong, and I'm sorry', and then share her fear as an explanation rather than a defence.

qa.q: What is Vaibhav experiencing when he writes 'Scared of me? That's worse'?
qa.a: Vaibhav is learning that his wife was afraid of him, which hurts on top of the secret; now he has to face both the hidden loan and the idea that she saw him as someone to fear.

grounding: Shows the wife's shame and loyalty to her family turning into the justification that her husband would never have agreed, which adds to his hurt.
